title: Derinkuyu's underground city
hook: A man knocked through a wall at home and found a city hidden underground.
peek: In 1963 a resident of Derinkuyu, in central Turkey, knocked through a wall during home repairs and found a tunnel. It led to an ancient underground city many levels deep, big enough to shelter thousands of people with their animals.
lede: Derinkuyu is a town in Cappadocia, in central Turkey. In 1963 a resident renovating his house broke through a wall and found a passage behind it. The passage led down into a huge underground city, carved by hand into soft volcanic rock, with many levels reaching roughly 85 metres deep. Estimates suggest it could hold thousands of people.

bullets.text: Cappadocia's rock is tuff, compacted volcanic ash that is easy to cut but hardens in air. That made it possible to dig rooms, stairs and halls by hand over many centuries.
The city has stables, kitchens, wells, wine and oil presses, storerooms and a chapel. Ventilation shafts bring fresh air down to the deepest levels, and wells reached water.
Huge round stones, like millstones, could be rolled across passages from the inside to seal each level, letting people shelter safely below in troubled times.
Nobody knows for sure. Digging may have begun in the first millennium BC, perhaps by the Phrygians, and the city was greatly expanded in the Byzantine era.
A tunnel several kilometres long is thought to link Derinkuyu with Kaymaklı, another underground city nearby. Visitors today can explore part of Derinkuyu's upper levels.
